blocks.text: The N Queens problem asks: place N queens on an N by N chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. In chess, a queen attacks any square along its row, its column, or either of its two diagonals, so a valid placement means no two queens ever share a row, a column, or a diagonal.

This is one of the most quoted backtracking problems in interviews, not because chess knowledge matters, but because it forces you to design and combine multiple independent constraint checks (row, column, two diagonal directions) into a single efficient search, which is a skill that transfers directly to many real constraint satisfaction problems.

A useful simplification collapses the search space immediately: since no two queens can ever share a row, you never need to decide "which row does this queen go in," you only need to decide, for each row in order, which column to place its one queen in. This turns an apparently 2D placement problem into a much simpler sequence of N column choices.

Because exactly one queen must occupy each row (N queens, N rows, and no row can hold two queens without them attacking each other directly), the search can process rows in order, 0 through N-1, and at each row choose exactly one column for that row's queen. This automatically satisfies the row constraint by construction: it is structurally impossible to ever place two queens in the same row.

What remains is checking, for each candidate column in the current row, whether placing a queen there conflicts with any queen already placed in an earlier row, specifically a column conflict or either diagonal conflict.

blocks.caption: A queen at (row, col) conflicts with any earlier queen sharing its column, or sharing the value of row+col (one diagonal), or sharing the value of row-col (the other diagonal).
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406864480-351377370.png
Column conflict: simplest to check, maintain a set of columns already used by earlier queens. Placing a new queen in an already used column is always invalid.

Diagonal conflicts: these use a small but powerful piece of coordinate geometry. For any cell (row, col), every cell on the same "downward" diagonal (top left to bottom right direction) shares the identical value of row plus col. Every cell on the same "upward" diagonal (bottom left to top right direction) shares the identical value of row minus col. This means two O(1) set lookups, one for each diagonal direction, fully replace what would otherwise require scanning the whole board.
Maintaining three sets, used columns, used (row+col) sums, and used (row-col) differences, turns every conflict check into three O(1) lookups instead of an O(N) or O(N^2) scan of the board.

The unchoose step here removes exactly the three entries that were added: the column, the (row+col) diagonal, and the (row-col) diagonal. Forgetting any one of the three leaves a stale conflict marker behind that will incorrectly block valid placements in sibling branches.
Tracing a 4 by 4 board (N=4) shows a genuine dead end and the backtracking recovery from it.

blocks.caption: Placing a queen at row 0 column 1, then row 1 column 3, leaves no valid column for row 2. Backtracking to row 1 and trying column 2 instead eventually reaches a full solution.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406864481-901563347.png

items: Row 0: place at column 1. usedCols={1}, diag1={1}, diag2={-1}.

Row 1: column 0 conflicts on diag2 (1-0=1... check against existing: row0 diag2 = 0-1 = -1, row1 col0 diag2 = 1-0 = 1, no conflict actually, but column and diag1 checks against col 3 succeed) place at column 3. usedCols={1,3}, diag1={1,4}, diag2={-1,-2}.

Row 2: column 0 conflicts (diag2 = 2-0 = 2, no conflict, but recheck col: 0 not used, diag1: 2+0=2 not used... continuing the search) every remaining column conflicts with the two placed queens on some row, column, or diagonal, no valid column exists. Dead end.
Backtrack to row 1, unchoose column 3, try column 2 instead. usedCols={1,2}.
Row 2: column 0 is now free of conflicts. Place at column 0.
Row 3: column 2 is free of conflicts. Place at column 2. Row equals N, a full solution is recorded: columns [1,3,0,2].

blocks.text: This trace is exactly why the row-by-row framing matters: the search never has to reconsider WHICH row to fill next, it only ever backtracks to reconsider WHICH COLUMN a specific row should use, keeping the recursion simple and the state easy to reason about.

In the absolute worst case with zero pruning, trying every column for every row would be N^N. The three O(1) conflict checks prune the search dramatically in practice, but the search space still does not have a simple closed form upper bound tighter than a loose N! (since at most N columns are ever tried for row 0, at most N-1 remain valid candidates typically for row 1, and so on), and real world runtimes are much better than this bound thanks to the constraint pruning eliminating huge swaths of the tree early.

The key point to communicate in an interview is not a precise closed form bound, it is that the O(1) conflict checks are what make the search tractable at all for boards up to size 8 or so, compared to a naive approach that rechecks the whole board on every placement.

blocks.text: Every solution to N Queens has a mirror image, reflect the board left to right and every valid solution remains valid. This means the search only strictly needs to explore roughly half of the possible columns for row 0 (columns 0 through (N-1)/2), and every solution found can be mirrored to produce its counterpart, roughly halving the search space when only the TOTAL COUNT is needed. Care is required for the middle column when N is odd, since a placement there can be its own mirror and must not be double counted.

This optimization is a nice detail to mention if asked "can you make this faster," but it is not required for a correct solution, and most interview settings are satisfied with the row-by-row plus three-set conflict check design covered above.

content.title: 7. Counting Solutions vs Listing Board Strings

blocks.text: A small, common variation asks only for the COUNT of valid solutions (N Queens II), not the actual placements. This simplifies the code: there is no need to track colForRow or build any output, the recursive function simply increments a counter every time row reaches N, and never needs to build or copy anything.

The other common variation (N Queens I) asks for the actual board configurations as strings, where each row is represented as a string of dots with a single Q character at the queen's column. This requires converting colForRow into N strings once a solution is found, a simple O(N^2) formatting step layered on top of the same search.

Forgetting one of the two diagonal directions: checking only (row+col) or only (row-col), but not both, allows queens to attack each other along the direction that was not checked. Both are required, they represent genuinely different diagonals.

Rechecking the whole board with nested loops instead of using the three O(1) sets: this still produces correct output but throws away the entire point of the technique, turning each placement check into O(N) or worse instead of O(1).
Forgetting to backtrack the three tracking sets when undoing a placement: leaves stale entries behind that incorrectly block otherwise valid placements in later, unrelated branches of the search.

Using a 2D used array of size N by N to track occupied cells directly, then scanning it to check conflicts: this works but is a strictly worse version of the O(1) three set technique, and reflects not having internalized why the row+col and row-col trick exists in the first place.
N-Queens: the direct application, return every valid board configuration as strings.
N-Queens II: the same search, but only the count of valid solutions is needed, simplifying the code by removing all board construction.

items: Can you explain why placing one queen per row eliminates the row constraint entirely, without any explicit check?
Can you derive, from scratch, why cells sharing row+col lie on one diagonal and cells sharing row-col lie on the other?
Can you implement all three O(1) conflict checks and correctly backtrack all three tracking sets on unchoose?
Can you adapt your solution to return just a count (N-Queens II) versus full board strings (N-Queens I) with minimal code changes?
